evidence.title: PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence.text:
Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications, including agentic generation, voice chat, and incremental content rendering.
In these settings, model responses are streamed to users as tokens are generated, rather than being presented only after generation is complete, shifting safety moderation from a post-generation task to an online streaming requirement.
Specifically, a moderation decision made only after generation completes cannot prevent harmful content that has already been exposed to users.
Effective moderation must therefore keep pace with token generation while introducing minimal computational overhead to remain practical at serving scale. Existing guardrails address this requirement through two broad approaches. External guardrails, such as Qwen3Guard [ Zhao and others, 2025 ] , employ separate models to classify user inputs and model responses.
Although they can achieve strong detection accuracy, they introduce additional inference costs.
More importantly, post-hoc moderation can only identify unsafe content after it has been generated, whereas streaming moderation requires frequent inference by a separate model to detect risks during generation.
Furthermore, operating outside the foundation model limits their ability to directly leverage its internal representations. Native guardrails instead exploit signals from the protected model itself. HiddenDetect [ Jiang and others, 2025b ] detects input-side risks before generation, while NExT-Guard [ Fang et al., 2026a ] monitors internal features at the token level.

These results demonstrate that native guardrails can achieve competitive detection quality while imposing limited overhead on large-scale model serving. Our main contributions are: We propose PGuard , a native streaming guardrail that leverages dynamic layer gating to extract token-wise safety representations from a frozen backbone. We further introduce complementary stateless and sequence-based modeling architectures to support both independent token classification and sequential risk modeling. We develop a serving-aware execution strategy that coordinates safety computation with the scheduling and execution mechanisms of model inference engines. Our SGLang integration supports both modeling variants while minimizing redundant computation and synchronization overhead, without modifying the inference engine’s codebase. We conduct extensive evaluations across more than 30 text and multimodal safety benchmarks and real-world traffic. Our analysis demonstrates the benefits of sequence modeling, characterizes the trade-offs between detection quality and serving overhead, and examines the complementary roles of native screening and external adjudication.

evidence.text:
As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge.
Conventional external guardrails address this challenge at the cost of additional inference overhead and a potential gap between their safety judgments and the backbone model’s internal representations.
Meanwhile, frontier foundation models possess increasingly sophisticated semantic understanding and rich internal representations, offering an opportunity to build safety capabilities directly into the backbone.
Motivated by this, we introduce PGuard , a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone’s intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without altering its original inference pathway or generation behavior.
Specifically, dynamic layer gating selectively aggregates residual-stream representations across layers to extract safety-relevant signals during both prefill and autoregressive decoding.
To balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, PGuard supports multiple representation-modeling architectures, including a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules.
Its design also accounts for the execution characteristics of LLM serving frameworks, such as SGLang, optimizing computation and data access to minimize additional runtime and synchronization overhead.

A position is flagged if the predicted probability of any risk category exceeds its corresponding threshold. A production-ready native guardrail must satisfy four design goals, which guide the design of PGuard : Competitive detection performance. The guardrail should perform competitively with dedicated external detectors. Native integration with generation. Risk scoring should leverage the backbone’s forward pass, enabling per-position detection during prefill and decode without modifying the backbone’s computation. Low serving overhead. The additional computation should contribute only a small fraction of the end-to-end serving cost, targeting a few percent overhead on production backbones. Broad risk coverage. A unified training framework should support text and multimodal inputs, jailbreaks, multilingual content, and emerging risks under a shared label taxonomy. Figure 1 illustrates the PGuard architecture. The frozen backbone supplies residual-stream features from selected layers. Dynamic layer gating fuses the captured features at each position, and the fused feature is modeled either by a stateless variant or by a sequence variant based on multi-scale causal EMA-attention or a GRU-based recurrent module. The risk classifiers then produce risk scores under the unified taxonomy during both prefill and decode.

evidence.text:
Based on these representations, PGuard supports two complementary modeling paradigms. The stateless variant classifies each token position independently, while the sequence variants explicitly model dependencies across positions to capture how risks emerge and evolve during generation.
We instantiate sequence modeling with multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules, offering different trade-offs between detection quality and computational cost.
To enable localized safety supervision without requiring exhaustive token-level annotations, PGuard adopts segment-level supervision, computing loss only at annotated positions and for tasks with available labels.
Our experiments show that sequence modeling improves response-level detection over the stateless variant across both text and multimodal tasks. Beyond detection efficacy, deploying native guardrails efficiently requires coordinating safety computation with the backbone’s generation process.
Mainstream language model inference and serving engines (e.g., vLLM [ Kwon et al., 2023 ] and SGLang [ Zheng et al., 2024 ] ) coordinate batching, parallel execution, and GPU synchronization to sustain high throughput.
Accessing intermediate representations and reporting risk scores introduces additional dependencies into this execution process.
In particular, poorly placed synchronization can stall active batches, making the resulting overhead substantially greater than the guard computation itself. PGuard therefore incorporates serving-engine constraints into its execution design. We integrate PGuard with SGLang, aligning risk computation and reporting with the engine’s scheduling mechanisms. The integration supports both stateless and sequence variants without modifying the SGLang codebase.

evidence.text:
For each position and task c , the classifier outputs a probability distribution P_{c}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t}) over the task-specific categories \mathcal{Y}_{c}\subseteq\mathcal{Y} .
A position is flagged for an unsafe category y\in\mathcal{Y}_{c} when P_{c}(y\mid x_{1:t})\geq\tau_{c,y} .
Each trained PGuard model uses its own calibrated thresholds, configured separately for query and response stages and for text-only and image-text inputs (Appendix B ).
During prefill, the query-side verdict is derived from scores at selected positions or their aggregation, depending on the application’s policy, and is available before response generation begins.
During decode, the hidden state at position t is used to assess the content up to and including token x_{t} , while the same forward pass predicts the next token x_{t+1} .
Verdict consumption is configurable at deployment: applications can selectively enable task groups and determine how flagged content is handled, including reporting, interrupting, or steering generation. To further reduce serving overhead, PGuard supports sampled scoring, exploiting the observation that safety risks typically manifest across phrases or passages rather than in isolated tokens.
Under this option, PGuard performs classification and reports risk scores only once every p tokens, skipping the classification path at intermediate steps (Section 3.2 ).
For sequence variants, however, the recurrent or attention-based state is still updated at every token, ensuring that each reported score incorporates evidence from the entire processed prefix.

For each position and task c , the classifier outputs a probability distribution P_{c}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t}) over the task-specific categories \mathcal{Y}_{c}\subseteq\mathcal{Y} .
A position is flagged for an unsafe category y\in\mathcal{Y}_{c} when P_{c}(y\mid x_{1:t})\geq\tau_{c,y} .
Each trained PGuard model uses its own calibrated thresholds, configured separately for query and response stages and for text-only and image-text inputs (Appendix B ).
During prefill, the query-side verdict is derived from scores at selected positions or their aggregation, depending on the application’s policy, and is available before response generation begins.
During decode, the hidden state at position t is used to assess the content up to and including token x_{t} , while the same forward pass predicts the next token x_{t+1} .
Verdict consumption is configurable at deployment: applications can selectively enable task groups and determine how flagged content is handled, including reporting, interrupting, or steering generation. To further reduce serving overhead, PGuard supports sampled scoring, exploiting the observation that safety risks typically manifest across phrases or passages rather than in isolated tokens.
Under this option, PGuard performs classification and reports risk scores only once every p tokens, skipping the classification path at intermediate steps (Section 3.2 ).
For sequence variants, however, the recurrent or attention-based state is still updated at every token, ensuring that each reported score incorporates evidence from the entire processed prefix.

evidence.text: The effectiveness of PGuard depends on the extent to which safety-relevant information is encoded in the backbone’s intermediate representations. Attacks that induce harmful behavior without producing sufficiently informative signals in the captured representations may evade detection. Deep role-playing and fictional framing are potential examples that warrant targeted investigation. Furthermore, adapting PGuard to a new backbone requires calibration-set pretraining for layer selection, followed by guard-module training, even when the new backbone belongs to the same model family. These requirements introduce additional costs when deploying PGuard across different backbones. Our current jailbreak evaluation relies on static benchmarks and does not establish robustness against adaptive attacks involving multi-turn interactions. Evaluating PGuard under dynamic red-teaming scenarios is therefore an important direction for future work. In addition, the framework leaves intervention policies to the deployment, motivating further investigation into how streaming risk scores can be translated into effective runtime actions. More expressive sequence models, including recurrent–EMA combinations and full self-attention, also merit exploration when serving budgets permit. Finally, we plan to extend the evaluation to larger backbones and additional modalities, and to release the guard models, benchmark pipeline, and SGLang serving integration alongside this work.

evidence.text:
We presented PGuard , a native streaming guardrail that operates directly on the intermediate representations of a frozen backbone. Through dynamic layer gating, PGuard aggregates residual-stream features from selected layers, enabling a trained guard module to produce risk scores throughout both prefill and autoregressive decoding. We further explored three guard configurations: a stateless variant and two sequence-aware variants based on EMA-attention and GRU, offering different trade-offs between detection performance and serving efficiency. Our evaluation across more than 30 benchmarks demonstrates that PGuard achieves competitive detection performance against dedicated external guardrails while consistently outperforming existing native baselines in aggregate. Its streaming predictions enable early detection of unsafe responses, allowing potential risks to be identified before generation is complete. Integrated into SGLang, PGuard incurs only 3.56% and 3.07% increases in TTFT and TPOT, respectively, across the evaluated serving configurations.
These results demonstrate the practical viability of native guardrails for online safety screening, while retaining the option of external adjudication for flagged traffic.
We are also extending the integration to vLLM, with adaptation work currently underway.

evidence.text:
Directly integrating a native guardrail into the backbone forward pass can increase serving latency, even when the guard head is lightweight.
The overhead arises not only from risk-score computation but also from repeated kernel launches, sequential state updates, and host–device synchronization. Stage-level profiling reveals two primary sources of overhead. The first is redundant work .
Under PGuard ’s sampled reporting policy, risk scores are consumed only at selected positions, yet naively executing the guard at every token incurs unnecessary computation.
The second is inefficient execution . Sequential state updates constrain prefill parallelism, small operators trigger repeated kernel launches, and host–device synchronization can stall the submission of subsequent backbone operations. We address these bottlenecks through coordinated algorithmic and runtime optimizations.
Specifically, we decouple state updates from risk scoring by computing risk scores only at positions selected for reporting, parallelize guard-state computation during prefill, move synchronization off the serving critical path, and fuse compatible operations to reduce kernel-launch overhead. Under a sampled reporting policy, applications consume a risk score every p tokens. Computing scores at intermediate positions therefore incurs unnecessary overhead.
We eliminate this redundant computation by decoupling state updates from risk scoring.

evidence.text:
We integrate PGuard into SGLang [ Zheng et al., 2024 ] , with runtime support for feature capture, per-request state management, and streaming risk-score delivery. The integration supports the stateless, EMA-attention, and GRU variants through a shared engine interface. Figure 2 illustrates the integration. At each selected layer, the runtime captures the same residual-stream representation used during training (Section 2.2 ).
For backbones that maintain hidden-state and residual tensors separately, the runtime reconstructs this representation by summing the two tensors.
This operation is performed solely for feature extraction and does not alter the backbone’s forward computation. The resulting risk scores are exposed as response metadata, leaving the original token logits and sampling path unchanged. PGuard integrated into the SGLang serving engine. PGuard runs as a side path of the backbone forward pass. Hidden states from the selected layers are sent to the PGuard head, which reads and updates a per-request state for the EMA-attention and GRU variants. The resulting risk scores are streamed to downstream applications together with the generated tokens. For sequence-based variants, the runtime maintains persistent state tensors for each active request in GPU memory.
Each request is assigned a dedicated slot throughout its lifetime, enabling state retrieval independently of changes in batch composition introduced by the scheduler.
During both chunked prefill and auto-regressive decoding, the runtime retrieves the state associated with the request, updates it with newly processed features, and writes the updated state back to the corresponding slot.
For the GRU variant, prefill does not process query tokens recurrently.

evidence.text:
Together, these changes avoid unnecessary host–device synchronization during prefill. During decode, we overlap risk-score delivery with ongoing engine execution and align result consumption with the engine’s existing synchronization schedule. Asynchronous staging in pinned host memory supports this overlap without introducing an additional synchronization barrier for score delivery. The guard head consists of many small matrix operations, each requiring a separate GPU kernel launch and memory access.
For small inputs, these overheads can dominate the actual computation and result in poor GPU utilization.
To address this, we fuse compatible operations into larger matrix multiplications. In the multi-task classifier, all nine task heads share the same input features. We concatenate the weights of their first layers into a single matrix and arrange the weights of their output layers into a block-diagonal matrix.
This enables all nine heads to be evaluated using only two matrix multiplications, rather than eighteen.
The fused weights are constructed once during model loading, eliminating the need for weight assembly during serving.
This design reduces kernel-launch overhead and improves GPU utilization. Together, these optimizations align guard execution with application reporting requirements while preserving complete sequence-state updates.
By exploiting parallelism, reducing synchronization, and consolidating small operations, they mitigate the computational and runtime overhead of native guardrail integration along the serving critical path.

evidence.text:
Safety-relevant information is not distributed uniformly across layers. At each capture layer, PGuard reads the residual stream , i.e., the tensor that enters that layer. The capture is read-only and adds no state to the frozen backbone. Training and serving capture the residual stream at matching layer boundaries, reconstructing it from separate hidden-state and residual buffers where necessary (Section 3.1 ). Let \mathcal{L}=\{l_{1},\ldots,l_{m}\} denote the set of capture layers. For a sequence of T positions, feature extraction produces a tensor {\bm{F}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times T\times d} , where d is the backbone hidden size.
In an MLLM, the visual tokens simply occupy positions in the same sequence as text tokens.
Thus, image and text evidence is fused by the backbone before feature extraction.

evidence.text:
Despite this progress, existing native approaches remain constrained by the effectiveness of their safety representations and the runtime cost of extracting and processing them. Our evaluations further show that existing native approaches lag behind leading external guardrails in aggregate detection performance while still incurring appreciable serving overhead. These limitations motivate a more effective way to leverage the backbone’s internal representations for native safety modeling.
The intermediate representations of a frontier foundation model encode rich semantic and contextual information about the content being generated, providing a natural basis for identifying safety risks without duplicating much of the computation performed by a separate guardrail model.
However, effectively translating these representations into safety signals raises two challenges. First, safety-relevant features are not uniformly distributed across layers or token positions, making adaptive layer selection important for effective representation extraction.
Second, risks may emerge from relationships among tokens and evolve as a response unfolds, which cannot always be captured by classifying each position independently.
Addressing these challenges requires both adaptive representation extraction and effective modeling of dependencies across token positions. To address these challenges, we present PGuard , a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail built on a frozen foundation model backbone. PGuard introduces dynamic layer gating to adaptively select and aggregate residual-stream representations at each token position, enabling the guardrail to capture safety-relevant features across different layers.

evidence.text:
The most discriminative safety signals can emerge at different depths across inputs and even across positions within the same input.
To accommodate this variation, PGuard employs dynamic layer gating in two stages.
During calibration-set pretraining, with the backbone frozen, the gate operates over a larger candidate set of layers, and the learned gating profiles determine the capture-layer set \mathcal{L} .
During full training and deployment, the gate operates over this fixed set and adaptively weights the captured representations at each position.
We formulate the gate over \mathcal{L} , with the same formulation applied to the candidate set during pretraining.
The gate computes a score for each position-layer pair: where {\bm{w}}_{g} is a learned projection and \mathcal{I}_{t} contains the indices of the top- L layers by score ranked by their scores at position t . During training, Gumbel noise is added to the scores before selection.
In full training and deployment, we set L=|\mathcal{L}| , allowing all captured layers to participate while retaining position-specific weights. The fused representation is then computed as yielding a position-adaptive soft mixture of the captured layer representation.
This gating mechanism allows a single training recipe to accommodate backbones of different depths by learning layer preferences independently at each position (Section 4.5 analyzes the learned gating profiles).

evidence.text: We measure the serving cost of PGuard with SGLang on L20Z GPUs. Appendix D lists the serving configuration of each backbone in Table 21 . Each run uses a concurrency of 8 and 256 requests per scenario. The input length is 2048, 4096, or 8192 tokens, and the output length is 512 tokens. Each configuration is paired with a run of the bare backbone on the same node, and the two runs alternate in order across 4 rounds. We report the relative increase of time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT), together with the relative loss of output throughput. The bare backbone and PGuard use the same memory fraction for static allocation. Table 11 reports TTFT, TPOT, and output throughput changes with each backbone’s best combination of optimizations across three backbones and input lengths of 2048–8192 tokens. Among the available measurements, the largest increases are 3.56% for TTFT and 3.07% for TPOT. For the stateless variant, the maxima are 1.54% and 1.78%, respectively; for EMA-attention, they are 3.56% and 2.40%. The GRU variant has maxima of 1.38% and 3.07%. Output throughput drops by at most 1.73% for the stateless variant and 2.26% for EMA-attention. Most entries stay below 2.5%, and all entries stay below 3.6%. We measure the serving cost of PGuard with SGLang on L20Z GPUs. Appendix D lists the serving configuration of each backbone in Table 21 . Each run uses a concurrency of 8 and 256 requests per scenario. The input length is 2048, 4096, or 8192 tokens, and the output length is 512 tokens. Each configuration is paired with a run of the bare backbone on the same node, and the two runs alternate in order across 4 rounds. We report the relative increase of time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT), together with the relative loss of output throughput. The bare backbone and PGuard use the same memory fraction for static allocation. Table 11 reports TTFT, TPOT, and output throughput changes with each backbone’s best combination of optimizations across three backbones and input lengths of 2048–8192 tokens. Among the available measurements, the largest increases are 3.56% for TTFT and 3.07% for TPOT. For the stateless variant, the maxima are 1.54% and 1.78%, respectively; for EMA-attention, they are 3.56% and 2.40%. The GRU variant has maxima of 1.38% and 3.07%. Output throughput drops by at most 1.73% for the stateless variant and 2.26% for EMA-attention. Most entries stay below 2.5%, and all entries stay below 3.6%. This overhead is small and acceptable for large-scale production serving. evidence.text: Overview of PGuard . (a) PGuard extracts intermediate representations from selected layers of a frozen backbone during prefill and decode. (b) Dynamic layer gating combines layer features for stateless, EMA-attention, or GRU modeling, and task-specific classifiers produce risk scores. Serving co-design integrates selective computation, parallelism, non-blocking execution, and fusion (Section 3 ). (c) Per-token risk scores are returned through engine metadata, and the application applies its policy when a score crosses the threshold.

evidence.text:
For sequence variants, however, the recurrent or attention-based state is still updated at every token, ensuring that each reported score incorporates evidence from the entire processed prefix.
The early-interception analysis in Section 4.4 uses the full per-token scoring trajectory rather than sampled scores. PGuard also supports a two-tier cascade in which the native variant performs token-level scoring on all traffic, while only flagged content is escalated to an external reasoning guardrail for fine-grained adjudication (Section 4.8 ).
